rationale: A wins because it keeps the story sellable without getting cute with facts. Its strongest line, "Duolingo says beta users talked to its AI character for nine minutes at a stretch," is cleanly anchored to the supplied metric and asks the right measurement questions. B has good bones, but "Duolingo says people are talking to its cartoon owl" puts the wrong character in the headline, and "live, unscripted spoken conversation" invents a fact the update did not give. That is how you turn a sharp angle into a fact-check problem before the reporter even opens the email.
gaps_in_A: "free beginner chess course" adds "beginner," which was not in the update. Small, but this is exactly the kind of casual embroidery that creates avoidable corrections.
"a usage number this beat rarely gets from a public company" is plausible, but not proven by the update. It should be framed as a pitch hypothesis, not a fact.
The chess angle is real but thin: "Duolingo, the language app, is now teaching chess" needs course detail or a named curriculum source before it is more than launch-day filler.
gaps_in_B: "cartoon owl" is wrong. The update says users video-call Lily, not Duo, and a wrong mascot in the headline is amateur-hour factual slop.
"live, unscripted spoken conversation" invents "unscripted." The update says live spoken video conversations; it does not tell you how generated, scripted, moderated, or constrained they are.

"Duolingo puts its most-criticized design behind a live voice interface" overclaims. The update says some educators criticized gamification; it does not say this is the company's most-criticized design.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is the wrong instinct. The update already has a launch peg; the founder needs journalist-fit-check and proof cleanup, not a fishing expedition for a better peg.
